questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend scoping the capstone to one simple signal on a single instrument, rather than combining several signals or a large universe?
options: Because combining signals is mathematically impossible
The point of the capstone is depth on the full pipeline (design through stress-testing), not breadth of ideas, and a small scope is genuinely completable with only what the course taught
Because larger universes always produce worse backtested results
Because this course never covered how to build more than one signal
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames the capstone's goal as demonstrating the complete pipeline end to end. A deliberately small scope (one signal, one instrument) keeps that achievable, while combining multiple signals or a large universe would shift the focus toward breadth instead of depth.

questions.q: In the worked example's position-sizing code, why is `target_position` shifted by one day relative to the signal and size_scale?
options: To make the code run faster
So the position actually held on day t is based only on information available through day t-1, avoiding look-ahead bias
Shifting is arbitrary and has no effect on the backtest's validity
Because pandas requires all Series to be shifted before use
questions.explain: The shift ensures the position held on any given day was decided using only data available up to the prior day, directly applying the look-ahead-bias and fill-timing discipline from Lessons 18 and 20.

questions.q: What does the volatility-targeting sizing approach, scaling by `VOL_TARGET / realized_vol`, actually accomplish?
options: It guarantees the strategy will always be profitable
It scales the position size so that realized portfolio volatility tracks a chosen annualized target, with a cap on leverage as a hard risk rule
It eliminates the need for any other risk rules
It converts the momentum signal into a mean-reversion signal
questions.explain: Volatility targeting, introduced in Lesson 10, scales a raw +-1 signal so that the resulting position's expected volatility matches a target level, with leverage capped (here at 3x) as an explicit risk rule rather than left unbounded.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the "cost shock" stress test planned for Lesson 32?
options: To check whether the strategy can run on a slower computer
To rerun the identical backtest with transaction costs multiplied up, revealing how much of the strategy's edge is sensitive to the cost assumption
To test whether the strategy works on a completely different asset class
To remove all transaction costs and see the best-case scenario only
questions.explain: The cost shock stress test reruns the same backtest with costs doubled or tripled from the base assumption, directly testing Lesson 16's point that realistic costs can turn an apparent edge into a real loss — and quantifying how fragile the edge is to that assumption.

questions.q: According to the capstone's stated rubric, what must happen with the results of the two stress tests?
options: They should be run and reported, but have no bearing on the final conclusion about the strategy
They should actually affect the conclusion about the strategy, not just be reported and then ignored
Only the cost shock test needs to be run; the adverse regime test is optional
Stress test results should be hidden from the final write-up
questions.explain: The rubric explicitly requires that stress test results actually influence the conclusion drawn about the strategy, rather than being run as a formality and then disregarded when forming the final assessment.
